# All-point pairing for centrally symmetric bodies; a depth-level obstruction

These are exact auxiliary results about two copies of a continuous body.
They do not assert a mixed-integer center or a bound for an arbitrary
compatible family of fibers.

Let `d>=1`, let `K` be a full-dimensional convex body in `R^d`, and
write `V=|K|`. For any point `y` define its absolute ordinary depth and
the identical-body paired cost by

    f_K(y)=inf_(u!=0) |K cap {u.x>=u.y}|,
    p_KK(y)=inf_(u!=0,t in R)
      (|K cap {u.x>=u.y+t}|+|K cap {u.x>=u.y-t}|).

All caps are closed. Their boundaries have zero d-dimensional volume.
The infimum over containing halfspaces equals the displayed through-point
infimum by moving the boundary to the point.

## 1. A centered strip maximizes volume

Assume `K=-K`. For `u!=0`, `s>=0` and any real `t`,

    |K cap {t-s<=u.x<=t+s}|
       <= |K cap {-s<=u.x<=s}|.                         (1)

Indeed let the set on the left be `A`. Its reflection `-A` is the
oppositely translated strip section of the same body. Convexity gives

    (A+(-A))/2 subset K cap {-s<=u.x<=s}.

If `A` has positive volume, Brunn--Minkowski gives
`|(A+(-A))/2|^(1/d)>= (|A|^(1/d)+|-A|^(1/d))/2=|A|^(1/d)`.
If it has zero volume, (1) is immediate. Thus no regularity or strict
convexity of the boundary is needed. The case `d=1` is also covered.

## 2. Exact paired cost at every point of a centrally symmetric body

If `K=-K`, then for every `y in R^d`,

    p_KK(y)=2 f_K(y).                                    (2)

Fix a normal and let `T(s)=|K cap {u.x>=s}|/V`. Symmetry and null
boundaries give `T(-s)=1-T(s)`. For `s>=0`,

    T(s+t)+T(s-t)
      =1-Pr(t-s<=u.X<=t+s)
      >=1-Pr(-s<=u.X<=s)=2T(s),                         (3)

where `X` is uniform on `K` and the inequality is (1). Equality is
attained at `t=0`. For `s<0`, reflection gives

    T(s+t)+T(s-t)
      =1+Pr(t+s<=u.X<=t-s)>=1.                          (4)

For sufficiently large finite `|t|`, one cap is full and the other
empty, so equality holds in (4). We have in fact proved the complete
fixed-normal minimization: it is `2VT(s)` for `s>=0`, and `V` for `s<0`.

Now put `s=u.y`. For `s>=0`, (3) is at least `2f_K(y)/V`.
For `s<0`, (4) has the same lower bound because `f_K(y)<=V/2`:
two opposite through-point caps have masses summing to `V`. This proves
`p_KK(y)>=2f_K(y)`. The reverse inequality follows by restricting to
`t=0`. For a body symmetric about a different point, translate both
the body and the point; all measures and cap families are preserved.

## 3. Arbitrary independent symmetric noise preserves every depth floor

Let `X` be uniform on a centrally symmetric `K=-K`, and let `Z` be
an independent random vector with `Z` and `-Z` identically distributed.
There is no boundedness, density, or moment assumption on `Z`. Then
the ordinary normalized halfspace depth of `X+Z` at every `y` is at
least `f_K(y)/V`.

For any fixed normal, condition on `Z` and average the two equal-law
shifts `u.Z` and `-u.Z`. Equations (3)--(4) bound this average below
by `f_K(y)/V`. This applies separately to every nonzero normal, and
moving a containing halfspace boundary to `y` only reduces its mass.
Moreover all hyperplane boundaries under `X+Z` are null by conditioning
on `Z`, so the closed-cap formulation is unchanged. This is a statement
about every deterministic point, not just the center of symmetry.

## 4. Being Gamma_d-deep is insufficient without symmetry or a centroid

One cannot replace the centroid in the general equal-body paired-centroid
inequality by an arbitrary point of ordinary depth at least `Gamma_d V`.
Here is a rational, full-dimensional example with a strict gap.

Take the square pyramid

    K={(x1,x2,z):0<=z<=1, |x1|<=z, |x2|<=z}, V=4/3,
    c=77/100, y=(0,0,c), Gamma_3=27/64.

Then

    f_K(y)>=Gamma_3 V,
    p_KK(y)<=105317 V/125000
             =2 Gamma_3 V-607 V/500000.                 (5)

For completeness the all-normal verification uses the exact scalar
reduction from `candidate cf676492f27e8f72`.
Under the uniform law write `(x1,x2,z)=(ZU,ZV0,Z)`, with independent
`U,V0` uniform on `[-1,1]` and `Z` of density `3z^2` on `[0,1]`.
A cap with positive coefficient of `z-c` has conditional probability

    phi(w)=[1-c^3/(1+w)^3] if 1+w>c, and 0 otherwise,

where `w` is a symmetric sum of two uniforms. If their coefficient
magnitudes are `A>=B>0`, its law is exactly the probability mixture

    integral_(A-B)^(A+B) Unif[-v,v] v/(2AB) dv.

The case `B=0` is a single uniform law; `A=B=0` is a point mass.
This identity follows directly by integrating the uniform density:
it gives the trapezoid density `1/(2A)` up to `A-B`, followed by
`(A+B-|w|)/(4AB)` up to `A+B`.

The centered-uniform average is

    Q(v)=1-c^3/(1-v^2)^2                    (0<=v<=1-c),
    Q(v)=[1+v-3c/2+c^3/(2(1+v)^2)]/(2v)    (v>=1-c).

The first branch decreases, and its endpoint exceeds `27/64` by
`66973/968256`. On the second branch,

    4v(1+v)^2[Q(v)-27/64]
      =5v^3/16+63v^2/200-123v/400+146533/1000000.

The quadratic part has positive leading coefficient and discriminant
`-9007533/100000000<0`; the cubic term is nonnegative. Thus every
positive-z-coefficient cap has mass at least `Gamma_3 V`.

For the opposite caps, write `psi=1-phi`. When `0<=v<=1-c`,

    psi(v)+psi(-v)=c^3[(1+v)^(-3)+(1-v)^(-3)]>=2c^3.

When `v>1-c`, the second term is one, so their sum is at least one,
which is larger than `2c^3`. Symmetry therefore bounds every opposite
cap below by `c^3 V`; this exceeds `Gamma_3 V` by `17329 V/500000`.
Purely horizontal normals cut half the volume by reflection. These
arguments include every through-point normal, proving the first part
of (5).

For its second part choose the vertical upward normal and the shift
`t=1-c=23/100`. The cap at height `1` has zero volume, and the other
cap starts at height `2c-1=27/50`. Their sum is

    [1-(27/50)^3]V=105317 V/125000.

The boundary square has zero three-dimensional volume, as required by
the closed-cap definition. A strict gap also persists with both cuts
proper: replace `t` by `23/100-epsilon`, `0<epsilon<=1/10000`.
The paired cost rises by at most `3epsilon V`, leaving gap at least
`457V/500000>0`.

This only refutes a pointwise strengthening of the paired-centroid
lemma. It is not a counterexample to OC. In particular the construction
does not claim that two endpoint copies can be used as all the integer
fibers of their convex hull when their base separation contains other
integer points.
